title: Caramel Pork Bánh Mì with Quick Pickles
dek: Savory-sweet caramelized pork, punchy carrot-daikon pickles, cool cucumber, and cilantro packed into crisp baguettes.
image_alt: Caramel pork bánh mì sandwich in a crisp baguette with pickled carrot and daikon, cucumber, cilantro, and chile mayonnaise
ingredients: 1 1/4 lb pork tenderloin, sliced 1/4 inch thick across the grain
4 demi baguettes or sturdy sandwich rolls (5 to 6 inches each)
1 tbsp sriracha, plus more to taste

instructions.name: Quick-pickle the vegetables
instructions.text: Stir rice vinegar, warm water, granulated sugar, and 3/4 teaspoon salt in a medium bowl until dissolved. Add carrot and daikon, press them below the liquid, and leave at room temperature for at least 20 minutes while you cook.

instructions.name: Build the aromatic base
instructions.text: Heat neutral oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add shallot and cook for 2 minutes. Add garlic and stir for 30 seconds, just until fragrant.

instructions.name: Sear the pork in batches
instructions.text: Add half the pork in one layer and cook undisturbed for 90 seconds, then turn and cook 1 to 2 minutes more. Transfer to a plate and repeat with the remaining pork, adding 1 teaspoon oil only if the skillet is dry.

instructions.name: Make the caramel glaze
instructions.text: Lower the heat to medium. Stir brown sugar, fish sauce, soy sauce, 2 tablespoons water, the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt, and black pepper in the skillet for 1 minute. Return the pork and its juices; toss for 1 to 2 minutes until glossy. Verify the pork reaches 145°F, then rest it off the heat for 3 minutes.

instructions.name: Toast and dress the bread
instructions.text: Split the baguettes without cutting all the way through. Toast cut-side up under a broiler for 1 to 2 minutes, watching constantly. Mix mayonnaise with sriracha and spread it over both cut sides.

instructions.name: Assemble for crunch
instructions.text: Drain the pickles thoroughly. Fill each baguette with cucumber, hot caramel pork, pickles, cilantro, and jalapeño. Serve immediately so the bread stays crisp.

why_it_works: A short room-temperature pickle softens raw carrot and daikon while preserving the snap that defines the sandwich.
Searing thin pork slices in two uncrowded batches creates browned edges instead of steaming the meat.
Reducing the seasonings with brown sugar creates a concentrated glaze that stays inside the bread.
swaps: Use thinly sliced boneless chicken thighs and cook them to 165°F; add 1 extra teaspoon oil if the skillet looks dry.
No daikon? Use thinly sliced radishes or double the carrot.
For a fish-sauce-free version, replace it with 1 1/2 tablespoons additional soy sauce plus 1 teaspoon lime juice.
storage: Refrigerate pork and drained pickles in separate airtight containers for up to 4 days. Reheat pork in a skillet over medium with 1 tablespoon water until steaming and 165°F; assemble only when ready to eat. Do not store filled sandwiches because the bread softens.
notes: Choose baguettes with a thin, crackly crust rather than very dense artisan loaves.
Drain the pickles well before assembly; excess brine makes the bottom crust soggy.
The pork glaze contains fish sauce and soy sauce, so season only with the measured salt before tasting.

faqs.q: Can I make the pickles ahead?
faqs.a: Yes. Refrigerate them in their brine for up to 1 week. Their flavor gets sharper and the vegetables soften slightly after the first day.

faqs.q: Is this bánh mì very spicy?
faqs.a: With 1 tablespoon sriracha in the mayonnaise it is gently spicy. Omit the jalapeño and start with 1 teaspoon sriracha for a mild sandwich.

faqs.q: Can I use ground pork instead of sliced pork?
faqs.a: Yes. Brown 1 1/4 pounds ground pork until it reaches 160°F, drain excess fat if needed, then add the glaze and simmer until glossy.

title: Spinach-Onion Cheddar Quiche with Flaky Crust
dek: A deeply savory, sliceable brunch quiche with jammy onion, plenty of spinach, sharp cheddar, and a crisp bottom crust.
image_alt: Golden baked spinach, onion, and cheddar quiche in a fluted pie dish with a browned flaky pastry crust
ingredients: 6 oz sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about 1 1/2 cups), divided

instructions.name: Blind-bake the crust
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 400°F with a rack in the lower third. Fit the crust into a 9-inch deep-dish pie plate, prick the base lightly, line with parchment, and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake 15 minutes; remove the parchment and weights, then bake 5 minutes more. Reduce the oven to 350°F.

instructions.name: Concentrate the onion
instructions.text: Meanwhile, warm olive oil in a large skillet over medium. Add onion and 1/4 teaspoon salt. Cook for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring often, until soft and golden at the edges.

instructions.name: Dry the spinach
instructions.text: Add spinach by handfuls and cook until wilted, 2 to 3 minutes. Transfer to a plate to cool slightly, then squeeze firmly in a clean towel. Chop; you should have about 1 packed cup. Removing water prevents a loose custard and soggy crust.

instructions.name: Mix the custard
instructions.text: Whisk eggs, milk, cream, Dijon, nutmeg, black pepper, and the remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt until no streaks remain. Toss 1 1/4 cups cheddar with the flour, then scatter it, the onion, and spinach evenly in the warm crust.

instructions.name: Fill without flooding
instructions.text: Set the pie plate on a rimmed sheet pan. Slowly pour in the custard, pausing so it settles around the filling. Sprinkle the remaining 1/4 cup cheddar over the top.

instructions.name: Bake and cool
instructions.text: Bake at 350°F for 38 to 45 minutes, until the edges are set and the center moves as one gentle wobble. The center must reach 160°F. Cool on a rack for at least 20 minutes before slicing so the custard finishes setting.

why_it_works: Blind-baking sets the pastry before the liquid filling arrives, keeping the bottom flaky.
Squeezing the cooked spinach removes the water that otherwise dilutes the egg custard.
A small amount of flour on the cheese helps suspend the filling and gives clean, tender slices.
swaps: Replace cheddar with Gruyère, Swiss, or a half-and-half blend.
Use 10 ounces thawed frozen spinach; squeeze it very dry and skip the wilting step.
For a lighter filling, replace the cream with more whole milk; the texture will be slightly less plush.
storage: Cool completely, cover, and refrigerate for up to 4 days. Reheat individual slices on a sheet pan at 325°F for 12 to 15 minutes, until hot throughout; avoid high heat, which can toughen the eggs. Freeze cooled slices tightly wrapped for up to 2 months and thaw overnight before reheating.
notes: A standard shallow pie plate may not hold all the custard; stop 1/4 inch below the rim and bake any extra in a greased ramekin.
Put the sheet pan under the pie plate before filling so you do not carry a sloshing quiche across the kitchen.
If the crust rim browns too quickly, shield only the rim with strips of foil for the final 15 minutes.

faqs.q: Can I bake the quiche the night before?
faqs.a: Yes. Cool it completely, refrigerate, and reheat uncovered at 325°F for about 20 minutes. A whole chilled quiche needs longer than individual slices.
The usual causes are damp spinach, underbaking, or slicing while hot. Squeeze the greens hard, confirm 160°F in the center, and cool for 20 minutes.
Yes. Grease a 9-inch deep pie plate, omit the crust and blind-bake step, and begin checking the filling after 30 minutes at 350°F.

title: Skillet-Toasted Tomato-Apricot Panzanella with Burrata
dek: Juicy peak-season tomatoes and apricots, crisp olive-oil bread, briny capers, basil, and creamy burrata in a no-oven summer salad.
image_alt: Tomato and apricot panzanella with toasted bread cubes, burrata, red onion, capers, basil, olive oil, and black pepper
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb ripe tomatoes, cut into 1-inch chunks
3 ripe but firm apricots, pitted and cut into wedges
1/3 small red onion, very thinly sliced
8 oz day-old rustic bread, cut into 1-inch cubes
1 packed cup basil leaves, large leaves torn

instructions.name: Draw out the tomato juices
instructions.text: Combine tomatoes, apricots, red onion, and 1/2 teaspoon salt in a large bowl. Leave for 10 minutes. The released juice becomes part of the dressing instead of making the salad watery.

instructions.name: Skillet-toast the bread
instructions.text: Heat 2 tablespoons olive oil in a large skillet over medium. Add bread and cook for 5 to 7 minutes, turning frequently, until crisp and golden on several sides. Transfer to a plate to cool for 3 minutes.

instructions.name: Whisk the sharp dressing
instructions.text: Whisk the remaining 3 tablespoons olive oil with red wine vinegar, honey, garlic, capers, black pepper, and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt.

instructions.name: Give the bread a short soak
instructions.text: Pour the dressing over the tomato mixture, add the toasted bread, and toss thoroughly. Rest for 5 minutes—long enough for the bread to absorb flavor while keeping a crisp core.

instructions.name: Finish with burrata
instructions.text: Fold in half the basil. Spoon the salad onto a platter, tear the burrata over the top, and finish with the remaining basil, the juices from the bowl, and an extra grind of black pepper.

why_it_works: Salting the fruit first creates a savory tomato-apricot liquor that seasons the bread from within.
Skillet-toasting gives day-old bread browned edges without heating the oven.
Capers and vinegar balance the sweet fruit and rich burrata, so the salad eats like a complete light meal.
swaps: Replace apricots with two ripe peaches or nectarines cut into bite-size wedges.
Use fresh mozzarella if burrata is unavailable; tear it small and add 1 extra tablespoon olive oil.
For a dairy-free salad, omit burrata and add one 15-ounce can of drained, rinsed cannellini beans.
storage: For the best texture, store toasted bread, dressed tomato-apricot mixture, burrata, and basil separately for up to 2 days. Bring the fruit mixture to room temperature and re-crisp the bread in a dry skillet over medium for 2 to 3 minutes before assembling. Fully assembled panzanella is safe refrigerated for 1 day but will be soft.
notes: Day-old bread is ideal because it absorbs dressing without collapsing; if your bread is fresh, toast it 1 to 2 minutes longer.
Use ripe but firm apricots so the wedges hold their shape when tossed.
Burrata is best added at the last moment; its creamy center should coat the salad, not disappear into storage.

faqs.q: Can I make panzanella without stale bread?
faqs.a: Yes. Fresh bread works after thorough skillet-toasting. Let the cubes cool before tossing so steam does not soften them.

faqs.q: Why add apricots to a tomato salad?
faqs.a: Their tart sweetness echoes peak-season tomatoes while the vinegar, capers, and black pepper keep the finished salad distinctly savory.

faqs.q: Can this be a full dinner?
faqs.a: Yes. It serves four as a light main. For more protein, add cannellini beans, grilled chicken, or prosciutto at the table.
